name: The Agency Operations System
tagline: Six procedures, pre-written from real workflows
oneLiner: The six SOPs a digital service agency runs on, arriving already written for your service line — and every line of every one is editable.
audience: Freelancers whose first $5,000 month keeps turning into chaos
Anyone about to hire and realising nothing is written down
Agencies where every project runs slightly differently
problem: The first $1,000 month is a problem of action. The first $5,000 month is a problem of systems — and the systems are six specific procedures, not a general intention to get organised. Everyone knows this. Nobody writes them, because a blank SOP template is one of the least inviting documents in existence.
solves: Delivery that depends entirely on you remembering how you did it last time
Onboarding that takes a week because nothing is documented
Quality that varies by how tired you were that Thursday
Being unable to hire because you cannot explain the job
inside: Stage — Hustler / Operator / Owner as a diagnostic, so you build the procedures for the stage you are in
Six SOPs, pre-written from real delivery workflows for your service line, all of them editable
The brief-to-delivery workflow with its timings
The monthly client cycle, step by step
An efficiency audit that finds what to systematise next
Export as documents you can hand to a contractor on day one
outcomes: Six written procedures, today, instead of six blank templates
A first hire who can follow the work without shadowing you
Delivery that survives a week when you are ill
usage: Open index.html and pick your service line — the SOPs arrive populated for it.
Do the stage diagnostic first. Building Owner-stage systems while you are a Hustler wastes a fortnight.
Edit every line. A procedure you have not corrected is a procedure you will not follow.
Run one real project against the SOP and fix what was wrong.
Export and store them where whoever does the work can reach them.
notFor: Solo operators with one client and no plan to add another
Anyone wanting compliance documentation — these are operating procedures, not ISO
proof: The procedures come pre-written from documented workflows, not from a model. They will be wrong about your business in places, and the edit boxes are where you fix that.

name: The Proposal & Contract Kit
tagline: Proposal, contract, change order — same numbers
oneLiner: One form produces the proposal, the services agreement, the change order and the emails that carry them, so the figures always agree.
audience: Freelancers sending proposals in a text document
Anyone who has done unpaid extra work because scope was never written
Agencies re-typing the same six clauses per engagement
problem: The gap between a good call and a signed engagement is four documents nobody enjoys writing, so they get written badly and fast: a proposal with a price, a contract from a template site with the wrong currency, no change order at all, and an email that undersells all three. Then the numbers in the contract do not match the numbers in the proposal, and the argument in month two is about which one counted.
solves: Proposals and contracts that quote different prices, dates or scopes
Scope creep with no mechanism to charge for it
Six clauses re-typed per client and forgotten in a hurry
The 24-hour follow-up that never goes out because writing it takes an hour
inside: One intake form: fee, dates, client, jurisdiction, scope, revisions
A one-page proposal with three tiers and an expiry date
A services agreement carrying the six clauses an engagement needs — scope, revisions, payment, IP, confidentiality, termination
A change order that prices additional work against the original agreement
The covering emails for all three, written from the same data
Print-ready output; nothing leaves your device
outcomes: A proposal out within 24 hours of the call, priced in tiers
A contract whose figures cannot disagree with the proposal
A written route to charging for extra work instead of absorbing it
usage: Open index.html and fill the intake once.
Generate the proposal and send it the same day. Speed is most of the win rate here.
On acceptance, generate the agreement — the numbers carry over automatically.
Read every clause and delete what does not apply to your engagement.
When scope changes, raise a change order rather than an opinion.
notFor: Anything over a few thousand, unusual risk, or personal data at scale — have a lawyer read it
Employment contracts, or jurisdictions you have not checked
proof: Not legal advice. This is a drafting aid built from general practice; contract law varies by country, by state and by the facts of your engagement.

name: Invoice & Payment Automation
tagline: Get it out right, then get it paid
oneLiner: An invoice that adds up to the cent, due dates derived from your stated terms, a chase sequence that writes its own emails, and a live picture of what you are owed.
audience: Freelancers whose invoices go out late and get paid later
Anyone who has never sent a payment reminder because writing it feels rude
Small studios with money owed across several clients and no single view of it
problem: Almost none of the gap between finishing work and being paid is a collections problem. It is a decisions problem: what to number the invoice, when it falls due, when to chase, what to say, what to charge for being late. Those get re-decided on every invoice, badly, under time pressure — which is why the invoice goes out late, the terms drift, the reminder never gets sent, and the money arrives whenever the client feels like it.
solves: Invoices that do not quite add up, or use last quarter's tax rate
Due dates invented per invoice instead of derived from a payment term
Reminders never sent because each one has to be written from scratch
No idea what is actually outstanding this week
inside: An invoice builder that reconciles to the cent, with tax and discounts handled explicitly
Payment terms set once — deposits, Net 7/14/30 — with every date derived from them
A chase sequence that writes each reminder, escalating in tone on a schedule you set
Late fees calculated rather than threatened
An ageing view: what is owed, by whom, and when it fell due
Print and export, with your own branding
outcomes: Invoices out the same day the work finishes
Reminders that send themselves out of a queue instead of your conscience
One number for what you are owed, and one for what is overdue
usage: Open index.html and set your payment terms once, in Settings.
Build the invoice; check the total reconciles before you send.
Let the chase sequence generate reminder one — send it on the day it says.
Escalate on the schedule rather than on your mood.
Check the ageing view every Monday. It takes ninety seconds.
notFor: Accounting or bookkeeping — this does not do your books
Businesses needing e-invoicing compliance in regulated jurisdictions
proof: The arithmetic is exact and the dates are derived from your terms. It does not connect to your bank, so payments are marked by you.

name: The Digital Marketing Toolkits
tagline: Eight tools for running a marketing service
oneLiner: Prospect scoring, five outreach scripts, an eight-step production workflow with real timings, six priced packages and the retention behaviours — as tools, not prose.
audience: Anyone selling social media management as a service
Freelancers who can do the work but not find the clients
Agencies pricing packages by copying a competitor
problem: The operational knowledge for running a marketing service exists — a method for finding prospects, scripts for approaching them, a workflow with real time estimates, priced packages, retention behaviours. It exists as prose you have to re-read every time you need it, which means in practice you re-invent it every month, worse each time.
solves: Prospecting by scrolling until someone looks like they need help
Outreach messages written fresh each time and sent to nobody twice
Packages priced without knowing how many hours they contain
Clients who leave in month four because nothing was built to keep them
inside: Prospect Audit — score businesses on four gap signals; the list ranks itself
Five outreach scripts, generated with the prospect's own gaps in them
An eight-step production workflow with real per-step timings
Six priced packages with the hours each one actually contains
Three retention behaviours and the four pitfalls that lose accounts
A content engine: niche scoring and article briefs
Reporting a client will actually read
outcomes: A ranked prospect list rather than a browsing session
A package price you can hold in a negotiation because you know its hours
A delivery month that runs on a workflow instead of adrenaline
usage: Open index.html and score ten local businesses in the Prospect Audit.
Generate outreach for the top three; send it the same day.
Price from the packages tab, not from what feels askable.
Deliver against the eight-step workflow and time yourself once.
Set up the retention behaviours in month one, not month four.
notFor: Anyone wanting the content produced for them
Agencies with an established sales system that only need more traffic
proof: The timings are the documented ones, not aspirational. Your first month will be slower; time yourself and replace them.

name: AI Automation Kits
tagline: The audit produces the kit, the kit produces the price
oneLiner: A thirty-minute audit script, ten ranked automation templates, a five-part proposal and the ROI arithmetic — as one pipeline instead of six lists.
audience: Consultants selling AI automation to small businesses
Anyone who can build automations but cannot price them
Agencies adding an automation line to existing services
problem: The highest-ceiling service in this whole field is written down everywhere as separate lists: an audit script, some templates, a proposal format, a pricing table, an ROI calculation. In practice they are one pipeline — the audit produces the kit, the kit produces the price, and the audit and price together produce the proposal. Kept separate, each one is a document you have to interpret under pressure in front of a client.
solves: Discovery calls that wander because there is no audit script
Recommending automations in the order you happen to think of them
Pricing a build by guessing at hours instead of at value
Proposals written the night before, from scratch
inside: A thirty-minute audit you can run live on a call
Ten automation templates that rank themselves against the audit answers
A fee that lands in the right band from the audit, not from nerve
A five-part proposal, already written when the audit finishes
ROI arithmetic in the client's own figures
Systems tab — the stage model, SOPs, value pricing and an MRR tracker for after the first yes
outcomes: A proposal ready before you leave the client's car park
A price with an ROI calculation attached to it
A recurring-revenue plan rather than a series of one-off builds
usage: Open index.html and run the audit live during the discovery call.
Let the automations rank themselves; do not re-order them by what you enjoy building.
Check the fee band against the ROI figure before quoting.
Generate the five-part proposal and send it within a day.
Once signed, move to the Systems tab — the second client is where the SOPs start to matter.
notFor: People wanting the automations built for them — this scopes and prices them
proof: The ROI is computed from the client's figures as they gave them. Nothing verifies those, and the proposal says which numbers came from whom.

name: Business Dashboard Templates
tagline: Ten minutes of figures, one working dashboard
oneLiner: Starts from the smallest set of numbers you will realistically write down each week and derives everything else — with the formulas and a spreadsheet to graduate into.
audience: Anyone running a business on the bank balance and a feeling
Freelancers who want to know whether the month worked before the month ends
Studios with six revenue lines and no single view
problem: Most dashboard advice lists every metric that exists, which guarantees the dashboard is never built: tracking forty numbers is a bookkeeping project, and you have a business to run. The alternative is to start from what a person will actually write down each week — a handful of figures — and derive as much as possible from those.
solves: Running on the bank balance, which lags reality by a month
Dashboards abandoned because they needed forty inputs a week
Metrics with no formula written down, so they change meaning quietly
Outgrowing the tool and having to start from nothing
inside: Six templates matched to business type: digital products, agency services, coaching, content, e-commerce, local service
A weekly input set small enough to actually complete
Every derived metric shown with its formula and its source
Trends that need only a few weeks of data before they say anything
A spreadsheet export, so when you outgrow this page you rebuild it in five minutes
Nothing uploaded — the figures stay on your machine
outcomes: A weekly number-writing habit that takes under ten minutes
Derived metrics you can explain, because the formula is on screen
An exit path to a spreadsheet rather than a dead end
usage: Open index.html and pick the template closest to your business.
Fill in one week of real figures. Estimates are fine, mark them as such.
Do it again next week. Two points is a line; four is a trend.
Read the formulas next to the derived metrics until you can explain them.
Export to the spreadsheet when the page stops being enough.
notFor: Anyone hoping it will pull figures from their bank or Stripe — you type them
proof: Every derived figure shows the formula that produced it and the input it came from. Nothing is estimated behind your back.
